chunks.title: Air bronchograms
chunks.text:
An air bronchogram is a branching, air-filled bronchus made visible because the
alveoli around it have filled with fluid, pus, blood or cells while the airway
itself stays patent. Normally bronchi are invisible beyond the hila, since air
inside an airway surrounded by air has no contrast. Seeing dark branching tubes
within an area of increased density is strong evidence that the opacity is
within the lung rather than in the pleural space, which is what separates
consolidation from a pleural effusion or a pleural mass.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: The silhouette sign
chunks.text:
Two structures of similar density in direct anatomical contact lose the border
between them. A consolidated right middle lobe abuts the right heart border and
erases it; a right lower lobe consolidation sits posteriorly, leaves the heart
border crisp, and obscures the hemidiaphragm instead. Lingular disease erases
the left heart border, left lower lobe disease the left hemidiaphragm. The sign
is therefore a localiser: which border has disappeared tells you which lobe is
involved, without a lateral film.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Consolidation does not mean infection
chunks.text:
Consolidation is a description of alveolar filling, not a diagnosis. Pneumonia
is the commonest cause, but pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage, aspiration,
infarction, contusion and some malignancies produce the same appearance.
Distribution helps: perihilar and bilaterally symmetrical suggests oedema; a
single lobe with a fissural boundary suggests lobar pneumonia; peripheral and
wedge-shaped raises infarction. A student who writes "consolidation" and
describes its distribution is on firmer ground than one who writes "pneumonia".
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Distinguishing consolidation from collapse
chunks.text:
Both produce increased density. Consolidation fills the lung but preserves its
volume, so the fissures stay in place and the mediastinum does not move.
Collapse loses volume, so the fissure displaces toward the affected area, the
hemidiaphragm rises, the hilum is pulled up or down, and the mediastinum shifts
toward the opacity. Volume loss is the discriminator, and the position of the
mediastinum is the easiest place to look for it.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Measuring the cardiothoracic ratio
chunks.text:
The cardiothoracic ratio is the maximum transverse cardiac diameter divided by
the maximum internal transverse diameter of the thorax, measured on the same
erect PA film at full inspiration. A ratio at or below 0.50 is normal. Above
0.50 on an adequate PA film suggests cardiomegaly, and the degree matters less
than the trend across serial films. The measurement is a ratio of two widths on
one image, so both must be taken at their widest points, not estimated by eye.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Why AP projection invalidates the ratio
chunks.text:
On a PA film the heart lies close to the detector and is projected near its true
size. On an AP film — which is what portable and supine radiographs are — the
X-ray source is in front and the heart is further from the detector, so it is
magnified, typically by 15 to 20 per cent. A low lung volume from a shallow
supine inspiration widens the cardiac silhouette further. A heart that looks
enlarged on an AP film may be entirely normal, so the correct report is that
cardiac size cannot be assessed on this projection, rather than a number treated
as if it were diagnostic.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Cardiomegaly versus an apparently large heart
chunks.text:
Several things widen the cardiac silhouette without the heart being enlarged: a
pericardial effusion, which gives a smooth globular "water-bottle" outline; a
large anterior mediastinal mass abutting the heart; pectus excavatum, which
compresses and displaces it; and adjacent consolidation or effusion merging with
the cardiac border through the silhouette effect. Before calling cardiomegaly,
check the projection, the inspiration, and whether the border you are measuring
is actually heart.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Nodule, mass, and why the size threshold matters
chunks.text:
A pulmonary nodule is a rounded opacity up to 30 mm in diameter surrounded by
aerated lung. Above 30 mm the same lesion is called a mass, and the distinction
is not pedantry: the larger the lesion, the higher the probability it is
malignant, and masses are investigated on that basis. Both are discrete and
have definable margins, which separates them from consolidation, whose edges
fade into surrounding lung and which follows lobar anatomy rather than forming
a ball.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Margins and what they suggest
chunks.text:
A smooth, well-circumscribed margin is more often benign — a granuloma, a
hamartoma, a cyst. Spiculated or irregular margins, with strands radiating into
the surrounding lung, raise suspicion of malignancy. Lobulated contours sit in
between and suggest uneven growth. Margin analysis on a plain film is a weak
discriminator on its own and is not a substitute for CT, so it should inform how
urgently a lesion is worked up rather than whether it is worked up at all.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Calcification patterns
chunks.text:
Calcification within a nodule is reassuring only when its pattern is one of the
benign ones: diffuse and dense, central, laminated or concentric, or the
"popcorn" pattern of a hamartoma. Stippled, eccentric or amorphous calcification
does not exclude malignancy, since a tumour can engulf a pre-existing
granuloma. Plain radiographs detect calcification poorly, so its apparent
absence on a chest film means very little.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Nodule mimics outside the lung
chunks.text:
Several things project over the lungs and imitate a nodule: nipple shadows,
which are usually bilateral, symmetrical and at the same level in the lower
zones; skin lesions such as moles and seborrhoeic keratoses, which have
sharp margins because they are outlined by air; healing or old rib fractures
and bone islands; and vessels seen end-on, which can be traced into a branching
vessel on careful inspection. Before reporting a solitary nodule, check whether
the opacity is truly intrapulmonary.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: A systematic approach to the frontal chest film
chunks.text:
Read the same way every time so that findings are not missed through
inattention. Confirm the patient, the date and the projection. Assess technical
adequacy: rotation, inspiration, penetration. Then work through airway,
breathing (lung fields zone by zone, comparing left with right), circulation
(heart size and contour, mediastinum, hila), diaphragm and costophrenic angles,
and everything else — bones, soft tissues, lines and tubes. Review areas that
are commonly missed last: apices, behind the heart, below the diaphragm, and the
periphery.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Assessing technical adequacy first
chunks.text:
Rotation is judged by the medial ends of the clavicles relative to the spinous
processes; rotation distorts the mediastinal contour and can create apparent
cardiomegaly or a false hilar abnormality. Adequate inspiration puts the
diaphragm at about the level of the tenth posterior rib or the sixth anterior
rib; a shallow inspiration crowds the lung bases and widens the heart. Correct
penetration allows the lower thoracic vertebrae to be seen faintly through the
heart. Stating the projection and adequacy before describing findings prevents
most projection-related errors.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Commonly missed review areas
chunks.text:
A large proportion of missed findings on chest radiographs lie in a small number
of places: the lung apices, obscured by clavicles and ribs; the retrocardiac
region, where a left lower lobe lesion hides behind the heart; the area below
the diaphragmatic domes; the periphery just inside the chest wall, where a
small pneumothorax or a peripheral nodule sits; and the bones and soft tissues,
which are easy to skip once a lung abnormality has been found. Satisfaction of
search — stopping after the first abnormality — is the single commonest reason a
second finding is missed.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Costophrenic angle blunting
chunks.text:
On an erect PA chest radiograph, free pleural fluid collects in the most
dependent part of the pleural space, which is the costophrenic recess. The
normally sharp, acute angle where the diaphragm meets the chest wall becomes
shallow and then disappears. Loss of that crisp angle is usually the earliest
sign visible on a frontal film. Roughly 200 ml of fluid is needed before the
lateral costophrenic angle blunts on a PA view; the posterior recess is deeper,
so a lateral film shows smaller volumes, from about 50 ml. A sharp costophrenic
angle on an erect film therefore argues against a large effusion, but does not
exclude a small one.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: The meniscus sign
chunks.text:
Free pleural fluid has a concave upper border that rises higher laterally than
medially, giving a curved meniscus rather than a flat line. This is a surface
tension effect at the fluid–lung interface, not a fluid level. A genuine
horizontal fluid level on an erect film implies gas in the pleural space as well
as fluid, which points to a hydropneumothorax, a bronchopleural fistula or
recent intervention. The meniscus is the sign that most reliably separates
pleural fluid from lung consolidation at the base: consolidation opacifies the
lung but leaves the lateral angle and the fluid contour absent.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Distinguishing effusion from basal consolidation
chunks.text:
Both produce a dense lower zone on a frontal film, and mistaking one for the
other is among the commonest errors at this level. Consolidation tends to have
an ill-defined upper margin, often contains air bronchograms, and follows lobar
anatomy with a boundary at a fissure. An effusion has a smooth concave meniscus,
no air bronchograms, and blunts the costophrenic angle. Effusions may shift with
position; consolidation does not. The two coexist frequently in pneumonia, so
finding one does not rule out the other, and describing which features are
present is more useful than asserting a single label.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Subpulmonic effusion
chunks.text:
Fluid can collect between the lung base and the diaphragm without spilling into
the costophrenic recess, so the costophrenic angle stays sharp and the film can
be read as normal. Clues are an apparently raised hemidiaphragm, a diaphragmatic
dome whose highest point sits more laterally than usual, and a widened gap
between the gastric air bubble and the apparent left diaphragm. It is the
classic reason a moderate effusion is missed on an erect film. A lateral
decubitus view, or ultrasound, settles it.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Pleural fluid on a supine film
chunks.text:
On a supine or semi-erect film, which is what most portable AP radiographs are,
fluid layers posteriorly rather than pooling at the base. The result is a
generalised veil-like increase in density over the affected hemithorax, through
which lung markings remain visible, often with a hazy apical cap. The
costophrenic angle may look normal. Because density increases gradually rather
than forming an edge, a substantial effusion can be overlooked entirely or
mistaken for underexposure. Always check the projection before concluding a
supine film shows no effusion.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: The visceral pleural line
chunks.text:
A pneumothorax is diagnosed on a frontal film by identifying the visceral
pleural line: a thin, sharply defined white line running roughly parallel to the
chest wall, with lung markings visible on its inner side and absent beyond it.
The absence of vascular markings peripheral to that line is the confirming
feature, not the primary one — hypovascular lung and overexposure can both mimic
it. On an erect film, air rises, so the line is usually sought first at the apex
and along the lateral chest wall.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: The deep sulcus sign
chunks.text:
On a supine film, pleural air collects anteriorly and basally rather than at the
apex, so the classic apical pleural line may be absent altogether. Instead the
affected costophrenic sulcus appears abnormally deep, lucent and sharply
defined, extending further inferiorly than the opposite side. The ipsilateral
hemidiaphragm may look depressed and the adjacent heart border unusually crisp.
Because supine and portable films are exactly the circumstances in which a
pneumothorax matters most, this sign is worth looking for specifically on any AP
film.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Skin folds and other pneumothorax mimics
chunks.text:
A skin fold produces an edge that can be mistaken for a pleural line, but it is
a broad band with a gradual density transition rather than a fine white line,
it often extends beyond the chest wall, and lung markings can usually be traced
across it. Clothing, tubing, bedding and the scapular edge do the same. The
decisive test is whether vascular markings genuinely stop at the line: if
vessels cross it, it is not a pneumothorax. Calling a skin fold a pneumothorax
risks an unnecessary chest drain, so the threshold for this diagnosis on a
portable film should be the presence of both features, not one.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Tension pneumothorax
chunks.text:
Tension physiology is suggested radiographically by mediastinal shift away from
the affected side, depression or inversion of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, and
splaying of the ribs. It is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should not wait
for a film. The imaging point for a student is that a large pneumothorax with
contralateral mediastinal shift is an emergency finding rather than a
descriptive one, and should be reported as such immediately.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: External artefacts that mimic disease
chunks.text: Not every opacity is anatomy. Clothing, jewellery, ECG electrodes and their wires, and braided hair all project over the lung fields and can imitate nodules, lines or even a pneumothorax edge. The clues are external: unnaturally straight edges or perfect circles, a density that continues beyond the chest wall onto the soft tissues or the background, and symmetry that follows clothing rather than anatomy. Before reporting a solitary opacity, check whether it respects anatomical boundaries. Removing the object and re-imaging settles the doubt faster than any further interpretation.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Empyema versus a simple effusion
chunks.text: An empyema is infected fluid occupying the pleural space, and on a frontal film it looks much like any other effusion: dependent opacity, meniscus, blunted angle. Features favouring empyema include loculation with a lentiform (lens-shaped) collection, visible pleural thickening, and adjacent consolidation from underlying pneumonia. The split-pleura sign is a CT finding, not a plain-film one. Because the film alone rarely separates them, the correct student report describes the fluid and its distribution, and notes that clinical context — fever, raised inflammatory markers, recent pneumonia — determines the next step, not the radiograph.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Haemothorax after trauma
chunks.text: Blood in the pleural space behaves radiographically like any pleural fluid: a meniscus on the erect film or a veil of generalised density on the supine film. What points to haemothorax rather than a medical effusion is context, not appearance — recent trauma, fractured ribs, a chest drain already in situ, or associated contusion. A rapidly enlarging opacity after injury suggests ongoing bleeding and is urgent. Describe the fluid accurately, pair it with the history, and state plainly when the film alone cannot distinguish blood from other fluid.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Interstitial oedema in left heart failure
chunks.text: In left heart failure the lungs show the backlog before the heart looks dramatically enlarged. Early signs are interstitial: fine septal (Kerley B) lines at the bases, peribronchial cuffing, and upper-lobe vascular prominence. As oedema worsens it becomes perihilar "bat-wing" consolidation that characteristically spares the lung periphery — the reverse of most pneumonias. An enlarged cardiac silhouette with small bilateral effusions alongside these lung changes strongly favours oedema over infection. Describe the distribution first; it is what separates cardiac from infective consolidation.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Upper-lobe blood diversion
chunks.text: On a normal erect film the lower-lobe vessels are more prominent than the upper-lobe vessels because of gravity. In early left heart failure this gradient reverses: the upper-lobe vessels become as conspicuous as the lower ones, termed cephalisation or blood diversion. It precedes interstitial oedema and frank consolidation, so it is the earliest plain-film clue to raised left atrial pressure. The sign is only valid on an erect inspiratory film — supine positioning redistributes blood to the apices physiologically and produces the same appearance in a normal patient.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: The solitary pulmonary nodule: what the plain film owes
chunks.text: A solitary pulmonary nodule on CXR is a finding, not a diagnosis. The plain-film report should record size (nodule up to 30 mm, mass above), location, margins and any visible calcification, then stop: characterisation belongs to CT. The single most useful step is comparison with old films — stability over two years strongly favours benignity, while growth demands workup. Multiple nodules shift thinking toward metastases, granulomas or vascular causes. A student who detects the lesion, describes it completely and states what comparison is needed has done the whole plain-film job.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note

chunks.title: Lobar pneumonia and the fissure boundary
chunks.text: Bacterial lobar pneumonia fills an entire lobe with inflammatory exudate, producing homogeneous opacity bounded sharply where the lobe meets a fissure — a straight edge that effusions and most masses do not show. Air bronchograms within the opacity confirm an alveolar process, and crucially there is no volume loss: the fissures stay in place and the mediastinum does not shift. The silhouette sign then names the lobe. A parapneumonic effusion often accompanies lobar pneumonia, so look for a meniscus alongside the consolidation rather than forcing a single label.
chunks.source: Chest X-ray Training Companion — authored teaching note
